prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose in which memory, the body and dream are built into a vast metaphysical architecture, in novels, poetry and shorter fiction.

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after the colleagues' arguments. On public knowledge, Cărtărescu's voice is recognizable at sentence level and in structure. The Blinding trilogy and Solenoid make memory, the body, dream and cosmology into one sustained metaphysical project, and his work began in poetry, which gives the prose its imagistic density. The case is formal and linguistic ambition joined to real imaginative depth, kept up from the 1980s to major late works. That is the sustained and coherent oeuvre the will's wording about work of an idealistic tendency and the whole body of writing asks us to weigh. The attribution is unambiguous: one author, one language, one recognizable cosmology. The citation can cover the whole oeuvre, with the large novels as the centre and poetry and shorter fiction as the foundation. Carson is a very strong rival, and I keep her as my first alternative. Her formal invention and intellectual depth are real, and Autobiography of Red and Nox are among the most discussed formal achievements in recent English-language writing. But her corpus raises a delimitation problem that Cărtărescu's does not: translation, scholarship, adaptation and object-book work sit alongside the original poetry and essays. I do not regard that as disqualifying, but it makes a citation for the whole oeuvre harder to draw cleanly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is translation dependence. The case rests on density, sentence-level patterning and rhythm in Romanian, and I can assess these only through reports and translations, not directly. A second concern is that the maximalist novels may lapse into excess or self-repetition across their length. If that is so, a citation for the whole oeuvre would overstate the consistency of the achievement. My knowledge of the early poetry and the shorter fiction is also thinner than my knowledge of the large novels. The committee should test whether the late work deepens the earlier project or only extends it.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first for formal reinvention tied to intellectual depth and emotional force. She also notes that Carson's translations of ancient texts sit at the edge of what counts as original literary work under Nobel's will, and that the committee would have to weigh this.
responses.response: I agree with the qualification, and it is the main reason I still place Carson second. The formal invention is real, and I do not read the translations as disqualifying. But the question is how a citation could be drawn so that it credits original poetry and essay rather than versions of ancient texts. I would sooner answer it by resting a Carson citation on Autobiography of Red, Nox and the essays, which would narrow the scope of the oeuvre being honoured. Carlberg's own translation concern applies equally to Cărtărescu, and I do not exempt him. The difference is that the open questions about him are about reading quality (translation, excess), while the open questions about Carson are about delimiting the corpus.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for an unmistakable voice and an encyclopedic yet personal vision. She also warns that some of the large, digressive novels may vary in quality across their length, and that the citation must rest on the whole oeuvre and not on the biggest novels alone.
responses.response: I accept both points, and the second affects how I frame the citation. I have kept poetry and shorter fiction in the wording so that the prize is not for the trilogy and Solenoid alone. I also share her concern about unevenness inside the long works, and I cannot settle it without close reading of the Romanian. Her point that Carson's weight in the canon is still debated is fair, but I would not decide the matter on that basis, because whether experiments endure is hard to know for living writers. The more concrete reason for caution is that Carson's achievement is spread across modes, so it is harder to say which part of it carries the prize.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Carson first for sustained intellectual and linguistic daring with lyric intensity. He notes that her allusiveness may narrow the readership the Academy would regard as essential, and that the case rests on a body of work rather than one title. For Cărtărescu he raises incomplete translation coverage and the risk of excess or repetition.
responses.response: I agree that the case for Carson rests on a body of work, and I find that persuasive. I am less sure about the readership argument, since difficulty and allusiveness are not a literary fault, and I would not hold them against her. I take his corpus-coverage point about Cărtărescu seriously, particularly the poetry. That is why I list translation coverage as an unresolved issue instead of treating it as settled in his favour. Where we differ is on weighing. For me, scale and sustained imaginative architecture count for slightly more than the genre-crossing range that I admire in Carson, though I hold that preference with some uncertainty and it could move with a closer reading of Cărtărescu's later novels.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She asks whether Carson's hybrid formats will last in the canon or remain influential mainly among peers. She also observes that Cărtărescu's late novels extend the earlier visionary vocabulary rather than repeating it, and that the long-term reception of his very large structures is partly open.
responses.response: I share her reading that the late Cărtărescu extends rather than repeats, though that is a judgment from public knowledge and not from a verified reading. Her question about the hybrid formats is the one I find hardest to answer for Carson. Durability cannot be settled now for either candidate, so I would not rest my preference on it. What I can say is that Cărtărescu's project has a more stable centre. I would also note that the closeness of the two candidates in opening support gives no reason for me to change my literary assessment of either. The committee should argue the merits of each oeuvre directly.

uncertainties: Cărtărescu's Romanian prose can be judged only through translations and reports; the quality of the original sentence-level patterning is unverified.
Corpus coverage is uneven: the early poetry and shorter fiction are less accessible than the large novels, and the poetry is less well known to me.
Whether the maximalist novels are sustained across their length or lapse into excess or repetition is unresolved without close reading.
For Carson, how to separate original poetry and essay from translation, adaptation and object-book work in a citation for the whole oeuvre remains open.
For Adonis, the achievement lies largely in Arabic prosody and diction, and translations carry it only partially, so my assessment of him is limited.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own work on the literary fragment, poetic nihilism and exile literature overlaps thematically with the fragment-based work of Carson and Adonis, and with the dream and metaphysical concerns of Cărtărescu. I treat this as context only, not as evidence of a preference, and the profile shows no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer.
